title: 5 Essential Skills to Build a Startup
summary: This video outlines five crucial skills needed to build a startup that makes $1 million a year, drawing on examples from companies like Airbnb, Fast, and StackBlitz. The creator discusses selling, discipline, building with AI, making content, and adapting to change as the core pillars for startup success.
key_points: Focus on five essential skills: selling, discipline, building with AI, making content, and adapting to change.
Skill 1: Selling. Airbnb doubled its weekly revenue to $400 by having founders visit hosts in person and take professional photos of their apartments.
According to a Gartner survey, 67 percent of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free experience, and 73 percent avoid irrelevant outreach.
Skill 2: Discipline. Maintain strict control over finances by keeping business funds in a dedicated account and setting spending limits.
Skill 3: Building with AI. StackBlitz built Bolt.new using AI, reaching $4 million ARR in four weeks and $20 million ARR in three months.
Test AI outputs by giving it 10 questions it already answers well plus one unknown, checking if it admits it does not know.
Skill 4: Making content. Post consistently on platforms like LinkedIn and YouTube to build thought leadership and attract customers.
Skill 5: Adapting to change. Respond to industry shifts quickly, as seen with Chegg losing business due to AI integration in search.
Use a structured method to track expected results versus actual outcomes for expenses like ads and software.
Test your product and selling skills personally before hiring sales representatives or taking outside funding.
content: A startup called Fast raised [music] $102 million and shut down the next year. That's the kind of money founders dream about raising, but it still wasn't enough to keep the company running. Money can't replace the skills it takes to build a business. So, if I were starting a company with the goal of making 1 million a year, there are five skills I'd focus on. Some of these skills are changing so quickly that what worked a year ago might already be outdated. So, I'll show you all five, plus [music] which one I'd work on first. The first one comes from Airbnb, back when it was a failing startup making about $200 a week. Skill one is selling. In 2009, their sales weren't growing at all. So, the founders went to New York and knocked on the doors of people renting out their apartments. They helped those hosts fix their listings and they took new photos of the apartment themselves. Joe Gibbia, the co-founder, later said those photos doubled their sales to $400 a week in about one week. The apartments were the same, but people looking for a place to stay could finally see what they'd be paying for so more of them book. That's the first skill, selling, and a big part of it is knowing what someone needs to see or hear before they say yes. In a startup, you're selling to customers first. Later, you're selling to investors and to the people you want to hire. But buyers have changed. In a survey released in 2026 by a research company called Gartner, 67% of business buyers said they'd rather buy without talking to a salesperson. And 45% said they'd used AI to help with a recent purchase. That means your website and whatever shows up when someone Googles your name are doing a lot of your selling before you ever get on a call. Garter also found that 73% of buyers avoid companies that send them messages that have nothing to do with their business. So a copypaste message can cost you the customer, but when you're new, nobody knows your company yet. Your first customers will come from people you reach out to yourself. Use AI to figure out who to contact and what they care about. Then write every message yourself and make it about a problem they have. If you don't take selling seriously, you can spend a year building something nobody will pay for. But hiring a salesperson won't necessarily help you either. If you can't sell your product yet, they won't be able to. Once money's coming in, the next skill is not to waste it. So skill two is discipline. Fast is a good example of what wasting money looks like. In 2021, they raised $12 million from investors. That same year, they made about $600,000 from their customers. But Tech Crunch reported that Fast may be spending up to $10 million a month. In a single month, Fast could spend more than 15 times what it made from customers all year. That's an extreme case, but it's why skill number two is discipline. You only spend time and money on things that work. Before you spend time or money on anything, write down two things. First, write down the result you expect. Then, write down the date you'll check if you got it. It works for anything, like hiring someone or running ads. Say you spend $2,000 on ads this month, expecting 10 sales calls. On your check date, you look at what happened. If the ads only brought in two calls, you either fix the ads or stop paying for them. You don't keep paying for them out of habit. Do the same with software, like the apps and AI tools you pay for every month. New AI tools keep coming out, and each one promises to save you time and money. Zyo, which tracks what companies spend on software, found that businesses don't use about 30% of the software accounts they pay for. To catch that, keep your business money in its own account starting on day one. Put spending limits on your business card so nobody can spend more than what you planned. Then once a week, take 20 minutes to see what came in and what went out. If something's about to renew and you didn't use it last month, cancel it. And when a check date comes up, see if you got the result you wrote down. That's a lot faster when your business account and your cards are all in one place. That's what a company like Row is built for. Row puts your business account or your company cards and your spending in one place so you can see where your money is going every week. And if you haven't set up your company yet and you plan to raise money from investors, qualifying startups can apply for Delaware Incorporation with the fee credited back if you meet the deposit and balance conditions right inside row in a few minutes without ever leaving the application. It's attorney reviewed and the account application opens in the same flow. Links in the description. Selling and discipline have always been important, but the next three skills move a lot faster. Starting with AI. Skill three is building with AI. Stack Blitz spent 7 years building tools for coders. After all that time, the team was getting ready to shut it down. Then an AI model called Claude 3.5 Sonic got good enough at writing code that they could build a whole product around it. In October 2024, they launched Bolt. You describe an app you want in simple words and it builds a working version. Within 4 weeks, Bolt was on pace to make about $4 million a year. About 2 months in, it hit 20 million a year with a small team of about 15 people. Because they'd spent years getting ready, they could move the moment the AI caught up. That's third skill, building with AI. Stripe looked at the top 100 AI companies that use it to take payments. Half of them hit $1 million a year in revenue within about 11.5 months. That's about four months faster than the fastest growing software companies a few years ago. Keeping up with AI can feel like keeping up with the Kardashians. Open AI and Google have each put out several big new models in the last year alone, and Enthropic has too. The setup you build in January can be out of date by summer. So, start with your product. Even if you can't code, AI tools can help you build a simple first version of it to show customers within a few days. Then pick one thing you do every week, like answering customer emails and let AI write the first draft. The hard part is knowing when it's wrong because it sounds sure of itself even when it's making things up. So before you trust it with your customers, test it. Give it 10 customer questions you've already answered well, plus one it hasn't been told how to answer. Count how many of its replies you'd send without changing a word. Then look at that 11th reply to see if it admits it doesn't know or make something up. Fix its instructions where it got things wrong and run the test again. Save those 11 questions because that's how you'll keep up with all of these new models. Every time a big one comes out, run the same test and only switch if it does better. When everyone can build a product this fast, getting anyone to notice yours gets a lot harder. So, skill number four is making content. Mauommo started base 44, an AI tool that builds apps without taking any money from investors. While he built it, he posted on LinkedIn and X about how he was running the business, even sharing how much profit it made and and how much he spent on AI. One post explained why he used Anthropics AI models on Amazon's cloud instead of open AIs. After that, Amazon invited Base 44 to show off its product at one of its events. Most of Base 44's growth came from people telling other people about it. It had 10,000 users in its first 3 weeks and about 250,000 after 6 months. Then in June 2025, the website builder Wix bought Base 44 in a deal worth about 80 million in cash. That's the fourth skill, making content. Because of his posts, anyone thinking about trying Base 44 could see who was building it and whether the business was working. Edelman and LinkedIn found that 73% of business decision makers trust what a company teaches more than its ads and sales materials. And you can't count on Google to send people your way anymore. In 2025, Pew Research found that when an AI summary showed up at the top of a Google search, people clicked a website link only 8% of the time. Without the summary, they clicked 15% of the time. So, start by posting as yourself with your name and your face so buyers know who's behind the product. Pick one or two places online where your buyers already spend time, like LinkedIn or YouTube, and post there every week. Say you sell scheduling software to dental offices. On a sales call, an office manager tells you her biggest problem is patients who cancel the morning of their appointments. Record a 2-minute video showing how your software fills that empty spot and post it. Now, every office manager with the same problem can see your answer before they ever talk to you. Once people find you online, the last skill keeps your business from getting left behind. Skill five is adapting to change in your industry. In April 2023, the homework help company CHEG announced its own AI study tool built with OpenAI's ChatGpt4. A few weeks later, CHEG told investors that ChatGpt was already slowing down how many new customers it was getting, and its stock dropped 48% in one day. A year later, Google started showing AI answers at the top of the search results in the US, and CHEG said fewer people were coming to its website. In February 2025, CHEG sued Google. That May, it laid off about 22% of its staff, and that October, it cut about 45%. CHEG knew about the change and it was already working on it and it still got hit hard. That's the fifth skill, adapting when your industry changes. Keeping up with the news is pretty easy. The harder part is working out what change means for your customers than changing what you sell before they leave. You also have less time to do that than you used to. UBS estimated that ChatBT had about 100 million monthly users only 2 months after it launched. Start with a short list of sources you trust, like two or three industry newsletters or podcasts, plus your competitor's websites. Set aside 30 minutes every week to go through them. You can use AI to sum up the week, but read the full story yourself on anything that affects your customers. When a new tool comes out that does part of what you do for your customers, try it yourself. Figure out what your customers might stop paying you for and what they'd still need you for. Then put more of your time and money into that second part. And every time you talk to a customer, ask what changed for them because they're the closest to the problem. Investors pay attention to this, too. The founders I see raise money before they're making any sales can explain where their industry is going over the next 10 years. If you skip the skill, you can end up selling something your customers can already get for less or worse, something they don't need anymore. So, how do these five skills work together? Say you're starting a company that sells scheduling softwares to dental offices. You build the first version with AI and sell it to your first few offices yourself. Their question turns into videos that bring in more offices. You keep costs low, so the money from those first offices covers your bills. And you keep an eye on bigger companies, so you're ready if they start offering the same thing. If you charge each office $500 a month, you need about 167 of them to make 1 million a year. If you can only work on one skill first, make it selling. It's how you find out if anyone will pay for what you're building. For the first 30 days, make a list of 50 people who have the problem you solve and talk to at least 20 of them. Ask them the last time the problem happened and what it cost them, and write down the words they use. After three weeks, ask for money. Even if it's a small paid trial or a pre-order. At the end of the month, ask everyone who said no what stopped them and use their words to fix your pitch and your website. And if nobody pays, you found out in 30 days instead of a year. Once people start paying you, you'll eventually have a big decision to make, which is whether to take money from investors. Fast took $12 million from investors and still shut down. So before you raise anything, you need to know what you're agreeing to. Watch if you don't understand funding, you don't understand startups next, where I show you what you give up when you take an investor's money. See you there.
